name: Absolute electricity use
unit: MWh/site/year; kWh/workload
boundary: Operational electricity for the named campus and reporting period; distinguish IT, cooling, power losses and other support loads.
method: Sum calibrated import and on-site generation meters, reconcile exports and storage, and avoid counting generator electricity twice.
frequency: Retain hourly readings where available, reconcile monthly bills, publish annual totals, and report missing intervals and estimated shares.
whyItMatters: Absolute demand determines infrastructure scale; an efficient facility can increase electricity use when workloads and installed capacity grow.
tradeoff: Reducing cooling energy may increase water consumption; distinguish genuine demand reduction from shifting activity to another facility or supplier.
decisionUse: Compare expansion plans with observed demand trajectories and separately assess which operational changes reduce total electricity use over time.
minimumEvidence: Campus boundary, meter locations, reporting dates, grid imports, generator output, storage treatment, estimation share and utility reconciliation records.
availability: EPRI supplies modeled state electricity, not site meters; literature benchmarks provide selected workload measurements, with no complete campus inventory.

name: Peak load, timing and flexibility
unit: MW; hourly MWh; verified curtailed MWh
boundary: Facility demand at the grid connection and relevant utility or balancing area, distinguishing contracted, installed and actual coincident peaks.
method: Use interval meters to identify seasonal peaks; compare dispatch events with documented baselines and report rebound demand after curtailment.
frequency: Archive hourly or finer data, review monthly peaks, and assess summer, winter and grid-stress events separately from annual consumption.
whyItMatters: Grid capacity and reliability depend on when loads occur, while annual electricity totals can hide concentrated local infrastructure pressure.
tradeoff: Shifting computation may reduce peak demand but move water use, latency or emissions to a different hour or location.
decisionUse: Evaluate interconnection sizing, demand response and workload scheduling with utility-specific constraints and tested performance rather than promised flexible capacity.
minimumEvidence: Interval load series, timezone, interconnection boundary, seasonal system peaks, baseline method, dispatched reductions, generator operation and subsequent recovery load.
availability: EPRI includes modeled peak GW and scenarios; this dataset lacks metered hourly loads, coincident utility peaks and demonstrated flexibility.

name: Facility overhead efficiency: PUE
unit: Dimensionless total facility energy / IT energy
boundary: Facility and IT energy measured over identical periods and declared measurement points; include all relevant energy inputs consistently.
method: Divide facility energy by IT energy, disclose metering category and weather/utilization context, and retain the absolute numerator and denominator.
frequency: Report annual energy-weighted PUE alongside monthly values; investigate seasonal changes and alterations in occupancy, IT loading or cooling operation.
whyItMatters: PUE isolates support overhead, enabling cooling and electrical-loss diagnosis while leaving workload usefulness and total demand to separate metrics.
tradeoff: Improved PUE can accompany greater evaporation or more wasteful IT activity; it does not establish lower total environmental burden.
decisionUse: Use PUE to compare operational improvements within compatible boundaries, paired with absolute electricity, water and useful-service output measures.
minimumEvidence: Facility and IT energy meters, synchronized periods, metering category, allocation for shared buildings, occupancy, weather and documented calculation method.
availability: The dataset explains PUE but lacks matched facility and IT meter series for Indiana or California project-level comparisons.

name: Purchased-electricity GHG inventory
unit: tCO2e/year; gCO2e/kWh, separately by method
boundary: Purchased electricity within the reported campus or organization; keep location-based and market-based inventories separate and disclose geographic matching.
method: Multiply electricity by documented grid-average factors for location accounting; apply qualifying contractual instruments separately, preserving residual-mix and factor provenance.
frequency: Publish annual inventories with factor vintage and contractual coverage; add hourly matching diagnostics when time-resolved energy and supply exist.
whyItMatters: Two accounting views describe physical grid context and contractual procurement; annual renewable claims alone cannot demonstrate carbon-free electricity every hour.
tradeoff: Contractual reductions may differ from local hourly emissions changes; renewable procurement also has land, materials and water consequences elsewhere.
decisionUse: Assess inventory disclosure and procurement quality without subtracting claimed avoided emissions or treating certificates as proof of local zero emissions.
minimumEvidence: Electricity totals, factor geography and year, gases and GWP version, instrument ownership and retirement, coverage gaps and accounting rules.
availability: Existing GHG guidance supports methods; no matched campus load, factors and instruments are available here to calculate audited site inventories.

name: Consequential electricity emissions
unit: Change in tCO2e versus explicit counterfactual
boundary: Power-system response to an identified load, siting, scheduling or procurement decision, over a stated geography and time horizon.
method: Model incremental generation and capacity changes against an explicit baseline; label marginal factors, dispatch assumptions and sensitivity ranges.
frequency: Assess each material decision; update scenarios when grid forecasts, load shape or transmission assumptions change, retaining previous versions for comparison.
whyItMatters: A decision can change emissions differently from its allocated inventory, especially when new capacity or different generating units respond.
tradeoff: Short-run dispatch savings may conflict with long-run infrastructure effects, local air pollution or water demand; scenario choices influence conclusions.
decisionUse: Compare alternatives with common service requirements and uncertainty ranges; report consequential results separately from location-based and market-based inventories.
minimumEvidence: Counterfactual, decision horizon, hourly loads, marginal-emissions model, capacity response, transmission constraints, model vintage and transparent sensitivity analysis.
availability: Marginal-emissions preprint offers methods; existing state scenarios do not identify causal grid responses or establish site-specific avoided emissions.

name: Embodied and full life-cycle GHG
unit: tCO2e/project; kgCO2e/defined service
boundary: Raw materials, fabrication, buildings, equipment, transport, operation and end-of-life; identify networks and user devices included or excluded explicitly.
method: Combine process inventories with operational data; allocate shared hardware transparently across service life and utilization, testing alternative lifetimes and allocations.
frequency: Update at procurement, retrofit and retirement, then reconcile annually with asset records and significant changes in utilization or supplier data.
whyItMatters: Operational decarbonization leaves equipment and construction burdens; omitting manufacturing can substantially understate the footprint of a specific AI deployment.
tradeoff: New hardware can reduce operational energy yet increase manufacturing impacts; lifetime extension benefits depend on performance, reliability and grid emissions.
decisionUse: Compare replacement, refurbishment and deployment options using equivalent service requirements, consistent system boundaries and separate life-cycle stage results.
minimumEvidence: Bill of materials, supplier inventories, asset lifetimes, utilization, functional unit, allocation rules, electricity assumptions, end-of-life treatment and uncertainty ranges.
availability: BLOOM and computing studies illustrate allocated life-cycle estimates; project bills of materials and comparable supplier inventories are absent here.

name: Direct fuel and refrigerant emissions
unit: Fuel quantity; kg refrigerant lost; tCO2e/year
boundary: On-site combustion and refrigerant releases from campus equipment, including maintenance and retirement; separate direct emissions from purchased electricity.
method: Calculate combustion from fuel records and factors; estimate refrigerant losses through charge, additions, recovery and inventory reconciliation by substance.
frequency: Record every refueling, refrigerant service and leak event; reconcile annual stocks and report testing, outage and routine operating hours.
whyItMatters: Backup generation and cooling-fluid leaks remain direct emissions sources even when annual purchased electricity is matched with renewable instruments.
tradeoff: Air-cooled or mechanical cooling may reduce water demand while changing electricity use and refrigerant exposure; backup choices change reliability and pollution.
decisionUse: Prioritize leak prevention and low-emission backup options; assess actual use separately from installed engine capacity and maximum permitted operation.
minimumEvidence: Fuel invoices, engine runtime, refrigerant species and charge, service additions, recovered mass, emission factors, GWP version and boundary reconciliation.
availability: Existing sources describe designs and reporting concepts; no complete campus fuel ledger, runtime history or refrigerant mass balance is included.

name: Direct withdrawal by source
unit: m³/year; m³/day; source-specific volumes
boundary: Water entering the named campus from surface water, groundwater, municipal or reclaimed supplies; report construction dewatering separately from operations.
method: Meter each intake, identify ultimate source and treatment, and distinguish withdrawals from storage capacity, sewer flows and water consumed.
frequency: Publish monthly totals, daily peaks and seasonal source mix; retain shorter intervals during drought, construction pumping or supply restrictions.
whyItMatters: Withdrawal indicates pressure on supply and infrastructure, but does not reveal how much returns or whether the source is locally scarce.
tradeoff: Reclaimed water can reduce potable demand while altering treatment energy and downstream return flows; source substitution requires a watershed-specific assessment.
decisionUse: Assess water-supply agreements and drought performance using actual demand by source, independently from treatment plant capacity and permit design maxima.
minimumEvidence: Intake meters, source identities, daily and monthly series, construction versus operation separation, estimation flags and utility delivery reconciliations.
availability: Google discloses selected 2024 campus volumes, sometimes estimated; the sample contains no Indiana or California campus water measurements.

name: Direct consumption and stated WUE
unit: m³/year; L/kWh IT, numerator explicitly labeled
boundary: Water not returned within the stated basin and time boundary; distinguish site water-input WUE from consumption-based intensity measures.
method: Reconcile withdrawals, discharge destinations and storage changes; divide the explicitly named water numerator by matched IT electricity for intensity.
frequency: Reconcile monthly water balances and publish annual WUE with summer peaks; separately report uncertain returns, storage changes and measurement gaps.
whyItMatters: Consumptive losses reduce water available to other users; WUE supports operational diagnosis only when its numerator and denominator are consistent.
tradeoff: Low site WUE can shift demand to electricity generation; low consumption does not imply harmless discharge temperature or chemistry.
decisionUse: Compare cooling alternatives using both absolute volumes and defined intensities; do not calculate WUE from state electricity and unrelated campuses.
minimumEvidence: Withdrawal, discharge and storage records, basin and timing of returns, IT energy, balance closure, water quality and explicitly stated WUE definition.
availability: Google provides withdrawal-minus-discharge estimates for named sites; missing matched IT electricity prevents comparable campus WUE calculations in this dataset.

name: Indirect electricity and supply-chain water
unit: m³ withdrawal and m³ consumption, separately
boundary: Electricity-generation and hardware-manufacturing water attributed to the service; retain upstream watersheds and distinguish these burdens from direct site water.
method: Multiply location-specific energy or material activity by compatible withdrawal and consumption factors; disclose cooling, hydropower and allocation assumptions.
frequency: Recalculate annually and when electricity sourcing, hardware procurement or operating location changes; use seasonal factors where validated data permit.
whyItMatters: Cooling alone misses water used by power plants and semiconductor production, potentially shifting burdens to distant communities and ecosystems.
tradeoff: Water-intensive clean electricity or fabrication can offset site savings; upstream allocation choices can dominate cross-location comparisons and apparent rankings.
decisionUse: Evaluate cooling and procurement together, reporting direct and indirect components and testing alternative electricity-water factors before selecting locations.
minimumEvidence: Energy geography, generation mix, water-factor definitions and vintage, supplier process data, basin assignments, allocation method and uncertainty ranges.
availability: Studies offer modeled indirect-water examples; supplier inventories and matched campus electricity are missing, preventing reliable project-specific totals here.

name: Seasonal scarcity and supply resilience
unit: Monthly m³; basin stress category; drought scenarios
boundary: Facility and upstream watersheds, local users and ecological flows during relevant months; distinguish water availability from treatment and pipe capacity.
method: Overlay source-specific seasonal demand with basin screening indicators, validated local hydrology and drought scenarios; avoid interpreting screening scores as spare supply.
frequency: Review seasonal conditions monthly, update drought assessments as conditions change, and reassess before expansions or changes in water source.
whyItMatters: Equal annual volumes can create different harms depending on dry-season demand, groundwater recovery, existing users and ecological flow requirements.
tradeoff: Lower-carbon locations may face greater water scarcity; annual replenishment claims may occur in different basins or seasons from consumption.
decisionUse: Screen sites, then request local drought-yield analysis, operating triggers and contingency plans before concluding that infrastructure can support expansion.
minimumEvidence: Source watershed, monthly withdrawals and consumption, competing demand, groundwater or streamflow data, drought assumptions, ecological requirements and local hydrologic review.
availability: Aqueduct supplies screening context; Indiana system capacities do not establish sustainable yield, and this dataset lacks calibrated campus water models.

name: Combustion pollution and population exposure
unit: kg NOx/PM2.5; µg/m³; separately modeled health outcomes
boundary: On-site engines plus attributed power-plant pollution and exposed receptors; separate emitted mass, modeled concentration, observed exposure and health outcomes.
method: Combine runtime and tested or factor-based emissions with dispersion and population data; validate concentrations and retain uncertainty in health models.
frequency: Log engine events continuously, summarize emissions annually, and sample relevant background, testing and outage periods with meteorology and receptor locations.
whyItMatters: Pollution burdens depend on where emissions travel and who is exposed; equal emissions totals can produce unequal potential health impacts.
tradeoff: Carbon-oriented scheduling or backup substitution can move local pollutant exposure; modeled health damages are not observed diagnoses or proof of causation.
decisionUse: Compare backup and siting options through exposure analysis; prioritize monitoring near sensitive receptors and avoid attributing individual illness without evidence.
minimumEvidence: Engine specifications, fuel and hours, stack tests or factor quality, meteorology, background concentrations, receptor populations and documented exposure-response assumptions.
availability: Health studies provide modeled burdens and research gaps; this dataset contains no causal epidemiology or campus-specific verified exposure series.

name: Residential noise and tonal character
unit: LAeq/Lmax dBA; LCeq dBC; spectrum and tonality
boundary: Outdoor and relevant indoor residential receptors exposed to cooling, generators and construction; specify background conditions, time periods and equipment operation.
method: Measure calibrated A- and C-weighted levels, frequency spectra and tonal characteristics; compare baseline and operating periods under documented meteorology.
frequency: Collect day and night baselines, commissioning measurements and seasonal operating surveys; investigate complaints and intermittent generator events with time-stamped records.
whyItMatters: Persistent tones and low-frequency sound can matter beyond a single average decibel value; facility-internal measurements do not describe residential exposure.
tradeoff: Quieter cooling or barriers can affect energy use, airflow and cost; acoustically equal levels can have different perceived characteristics.
decisionUse: Assess design mitigation and actual neighbor experience against verified local criteria; do not import occupational limits as residential standards.
minimumEvidence: Receptor map, calibrated instruments, LAeq and maximum periods, LCeq, frequency bands, background subtraction, meteorology, runtime and applicable local criteria.
availability: Community studies identify concerns; no standardized Indiana or California receptor measurements are included, so compliance or health effects cannot be scored.

name: Effluent heat and chemistry
unit: m³/day; °C/temperature rise; pH; mg/L and kg/day
boundary: Campus wastewater, cooling blowdown and receiving treatment or water bodies; distinguish sewer design capacity from measured outfall quality and quantity.
method: Pair flow with temperature and chemical sampling to calculate loads; evaluate receiving-water conditions, treatment performance and source-specific chemicals used.
frequency: Follow applicable permit schedules; proposed assessment adds representative seasonal and upset-event samples, with continuous flow and temperature where feasible.
whyItMatters: Returning water does not eliminate impacts if temperature, salts, biocides or other constituents affect treatment systems or aquatic ecosystems.
tradeoff: Water reuse can reduce withdrawal while concentrating constituents and increasing treatment demand; disposal pathways determine where remaining burdens occur.
decisionUse: Evaluate cooling and wastewater designs using measured loads and receiving conditions; obtain the specific permit before assessing compliance or limits.
minimumEvidence: Actual flow, sampling location and method, temperature, chemistry, chemical inventory, receiving conditions, treatment destination, laboratory quality controls and applicable permit.
availability: Indiana sewer approval supplies design flows only; no campus discharge temperature, chemistry or receiving-water monitoring is available in this dataset.

name: Land change and biodiversity
unit: Hectares disturbed; habitat condition and connectivity indicators
boundary: Campus, substations, transmission, generation and relevant supply-chain land; distinguish previously developed land, sensitive habitats and indirect infrastructure changes.
method: Compare mapped pre-project land cover with surveyed habitat and post-project conditions; report fragmentation and species-specific findings without collapsing ecological differences.
frequency: Establish a preconstruction baseline, monitor construction and restoration, then survey appropriate ecological seasons after operation and major site changes.
whyItMatters: A small campus footprint can depend on extensive infrastructure or affect connected habitats; hectares alone omit ecological condition and sensitivity.
tradeoff: Renewable generation and grid upgrades can reduce operational carbon while expanding land demand; restoration pledges require location-specific outcome verification.
decisionUse: Compare siting alternatives and avoidance measures using habitat evidence; keep biodiversity conclusions distinct from greenhouse-gas or fiscal performance.
minimumEvidence: Project and associated infrastructure maps, baseline land cover, seasonal habitat surveys, connectivity assessment, mitigation commitments and independently checked restoration outcomes.
availability: The present dataset lacks parcel-level ecological baselines or infrastructure footprints; this domain remains an unfilled project-assessment requirement, not zero impact.

name: Hardware turnover, e-waste and critical materials
unit: Tonnes/year by route; lifetime years; material-specific kg
boundary: Servers, accelerators, storage, network equipment and batteries from procurement through reuse, recycling and final disposal, including material supply chains.
method: Reconcile asset and mass inventories; track service life, reuse destination and recovery by material, distinguishing collection claims from verified recycling outcomes.
frequency: Record procurement and retirement events, audit downstream transfers annually, and update material inventories when equipment configurations or suppliers change.
whyItMatters: Rapid hardware replacement increases manufacturing demand and waste; critical-material recovery and safe handling depend on traceable downstream processes.
tradeoff: Extending hardware life can reduce manufacturing demand while increasing operational energy; recycling rates alone can conceal losses of specific critical materials.
decisionUse: Choose repair, refurbishment and procurement options using life-cycle comparisons; require downstream documentation and material-specific reporting for retired assets.
minimumEvidence: Asset register, equipment mass and composition, actual lifetimes, refurbishment records, waste manifests, downstream destinations and evidence of material recovery.
availability: Generative-AI research supplies global waste scenarios; no local asset mass balance or verified supplier and recycler chain is included.

name: Cumulative burden and distributional equity
unit: Separate exposure indicators by population and geography
boundary: Nearby residents, workers and upstream communities, including sensitive populations; compare distribution of burdens and benefits within a defined assessment geography.
method: Overlay measured or modeled exposures with demographic vulnerability and existing burdens; involve residents and preserve each indicator rather than inventing a composite.
frequency: Assess before siting, update annually with disclosed data vintages, and review when exposures, population conditions or expansion plans materially change.
whyItMatters: A project-wide average can hide disproportionate burdens on particular neighborhoods or workers, while benefits may accrue to different populations.
tradeoff: Low statewide carbon can coexist with local pollution or water hardship; screening percentiles do not prove project-attributable illness or individual exposure.
decisionUse: Identify priority monitoring and mitigation areas through source-specific analysis and community participation; avoid transferring California percentile ranks to Indiana.
minimumEvidence: Spatial exposure estimates, background burden, population and worker characteristics, data vintages, community input, geographic uncertainty and separately reported benefits.
availability: CalEnviroScreen 5.0 supports California screening, but no campus-to-tract overlay or community exposure inventory has been completed in this dataset.

name: Public costs, jobs and fiscal distribution
unit: Inflation-stated dollars; job-years; permanent FTE; rate effects
boundary: Public budgets, utility customers, workers and host community over the project life; distinguish private investment from net local public benefit.
method: Compare verified taxes and payroll with incentives, infrastructure, services and stranded-cost scenarios; separate construction job-years from ongoing full-time employment.
frequency: Assess before agreements, verify annual realized jobs and revenue, and stress-test delay, closure or lower-than-promised demand throughout contract periods.
whyItMatters: Large announced investment does not establish net community benefit; infrastructure costs and financial risks can shift among customers and taxpayers.
tradeoff: Jobs and revenue may coexist with environmental burdens; monetizing selected harms cannot replace separate health, water or biodiversity assessment.
decisionUse: Evaluate benefit agreements and utility cost allocation using common fiscal assumptions, distribution tables and documented responsibilities if projects underperform.
minimumEvidence: Executed agreements, incentive schedules, verified payroll and employment, actual tax receipts, upgrade costs, financing terms and utility cost-allocation evidence.
availability: Indiana announcements provide job and tax commitments; tariff examples show allocation mechanisms, but no independent project net-benefit calculation is available.

name: Disclosure, verification and accountability
unit: Coverage percentages; reporting lag; unresolved cases and resolution time
boundary: Every reported metric, campus boundary and affected community; assess data completeness and accountability separately from environmental performance itself.
method: Track missing data, measurement versus estimation, assurance scope, public access and complaint outcomes; preserve versioned sources and correction histories.
frequency: Update a public ledger quarterly where feasible, reconcile annually, and disclose material boundary changes, incidents and corrections promptly.
whyItMatters: Comparisons fail when reporting omits campuses or changes definitions; clear evidence status prevents promises and design permits becoming apparent measurements.
tradeoff: More reporting improves scrutiny but has costs and confidentiality constraints; redaction should preserve decision-relevant aggregates and transparent explanations for gaps.
decisionUse: Set procurement and community reporting expectations, identify evidence gaps, and assign responsible owners without treating disclosure quality as low environmental impact.
minimumEvidence: Metric definitions, coverage denominator, data owner, reporting dates, raw-to-reported reconciliation, estimation flags, independent review scope and complaint-response records.
availability: This review preserves source status and uncertainty; project-level reporting coverage, regular complaint logs and independent assurance remain incomplete.

name: Useful AI service and rebound
unit: kWh/accepted task; service quality; total annual footprint
boundary: Equivalent end-user service across training, tuning, inference, idle capacity and associated equipment; include deployment volume and any claimed downstream benefit.
method: Measure energy for fixed quality and latency requirements, then multiply by actual volume; test counterfactual savings and induced additional demand.
frequency: Benchmark before selection, remeasure after model or hardware changes, and review monthly service volume and annual operational and embodied totals.
whyItMatters: Lower energy per request can coincide with higher total demand; comparing unequal tasks or unconstrained output lengths can mislead procurement.
tradeoff: Smaller models, caching and batching may change quality, privacy or latency; efficiency gains may stimulate demand that erodes aggregate savings.
decisionUse: Procure the least-burden option meeting service requirements, monitor absolute budgets, and report avoided impacts separately with a defensible baseline.
minimumEvidence: Representative task set, acceptance criteria, model and hardware versions, tokens, batch size, latency, energy boundary, utilization and annual workload volume.
availability: Published benchmarks and BLOOM illustrate bounded cases; this dataset cannot rank current vendors or calculate a universal footprint per prompt.
